vignette: He stands twenty feet from the intersection, holding a paper cup of coffee from his shift at the fast food restaurant. He is forty-one, single, and of Lebanese descent, living alone in a studio apartment that feels increasingly like a holding cell. It is a Tuesday morning, and he is on his fifteen-minute break when a black sedan screeches to a halt outside the corner gas station. Two men burst out, waving firearms, shouting in rapid, unfamiliar dialects. He watches as the clerk behind the glass drops to the floor, pressing his palms against his head, while the robbers dump cash drawers into bags. One man kicks a customer who has tried to intervene. He stays frozen, his breath catching in his throat, listening to the distant wail of sirens before his legs finally carry him to a nearby car. The days that follow dissolve into a blur of fluorescent lights and repetitive motions. At work, he still flips burgers and bags fries, but his hands tremble whenever a customer's car pulls up to the drive-thru. He stops answering the intercom for a second too long, forcing himself to remember his name, his shift, his purpose. Nights bring no relief. He lies awake, staring at the ceiling, replaying the scene in fragmented loops. When he finally sleeps, it is fitful, punctuated by dreams where the headlights blind him and the shouting echoes in his apartment. He wakes sweating, heart hammering against his ribs, convinced the men are still there. He stops going to the gas station across from the restaurant. He tells his manager he prefers the evening shift, though it means working without the brief window of daylight he once relies on. He moves through his weeks with a quiet, exhausted precision. He avoids crowded areas, slipping into the back alley behind the restaurant when the lunch rush peaks. The smell of frying oil, once comforting, now triggers a tightness in his chest that makes it hard to breathe. He checks the locks on his apartment door six times before leaving. He tells coworkers he is tired, that he just needs rest, but the truth is heavier. He feels detached from his own life, watching himself move through routines like a ghost. When his mother calls from Beirut, her voice crackling through the speakerphone, he answers politely but cuts the conversation short, unable to bear the normalcy of her questions about his health, his sleep, his friends. He lives alone, and finds it easier that way. In our sessions, he sits on the edge of the chair, hands clasped tightly in his lap. He speaks in a low, steady voice, but his eyes dart toward the window with every passing car. He describes how he now times his commute to avoid rush hour, how he scans parking lots before stepping out of his vehicle, how he flinches at sudden noises like dropped trays or slamming doors. He admits he no longer enjoys the food he serves, that every meal tastes like ash. He worries he will never feel safe again. When I ask about the past, he speaks of the man who kicks the customer, of the clerk's trembling hands, of his own paralyzed stillness. He carries the weight of what he saw, the unspoken question of why he was spared, the quiet shame of not acting. He does not look at me when he says it. He just watches the street outside, waiting for the next shift, the next night, the next day to pass.
